To unfrock someone means to officially strip a priest, monk, or religious minister of their clerical status — removing them from their position in the Church as a punishment, and taking away all the authority, rights, and privileges that came with it.

To understand this word fully, you first need to understand what a priest actually has by virtue of being a priest. A person ordained into the clergy holds a special, formal standing within their religious institution. They are authorized to perform sacraments (such as Mass, baptism, and confession in the Catholic Church), they carry religious titles like "Father" or "Reverend," they can hold positions of authority, and they represent their institution officially.

When a priest is unfrocked, every single one of those things is taken away. They are no longer recognized as a priest by their Church. Their clerical authority is nullified. They lose their title. They can no longer perform sacraments or official religious duties. In the eyes of the Church, they are reduced to the status of an ordinary layperson — as if they were never ordained.

Being unfrocked is one of the most severe punishments a religious institution can impose on one of its own. It does not happen for minor infractions. A priest or minister is typically unfrocked after committing a very serious offense — such as sexual abuse, grave moral misconduct, heresy (holding beliefs that fundamentally contradict the Church's doctrine), or a major violation of Church law or ethics.

It follows an official investigation or formal proceedings within the institution. It is deliberate, considered, and serious.
Three Crucial Things to Understand About the Word

First: it is a punishment, not a resignation. This is a very important distinction. If a priest voluntarily leaves the clergy — perhaps because they want to marry, or simply because they no longer want to serve — we do not say they were "unfrocked." That would be a voluntary departure. The word "unfrock" specifically implies that the removal was forced upon the person, usually because of wrongdoing. The person did not choose it; it was done to them.

Second: it is institutional. A priest cannot unfrock themselves, and an outsider cannot unfrock a priest either. The power to unfrock someone rests entirely with the religious institution itself — in the Catholic Church, ultimately with the Vatican; in Protestant denominations, with the relevant governing body or leadership. It is always a formal, top-down, official act.

Third: it is effectively permanent. Being unfrocked is not a temporary suspension or a time-out. It is a definitive removal from clerical status. While reinstatement is theoretically possible in some denominations under exceptional circumstances, unfrocking is understood to be a lasting — and extremely serious — consequence.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

You will most commonly see "unfrock" in the passive voice, because the action is something done to a person by an institution, not something the person does themselves:

  • "The priest was unfrocked after the investigation confirmed the allegations against him."
  • "He was unfrocked by the Vatican following the scandal."

You will occasionally see it in the active voice, where the institution is the subject:

  • "The Church unfrocked the bishop after years of misconduct."

Both are correct. The passive is simply more common because it reflects the nature of the act — the person receiving it is the focus.

Because "unfrock" carries such a strong sense of stripping someone of their professional standing and authority as a punishment, it is sometimes borrowed and used figuratively — outside the religious world — to describe removing someone from any position of power or trust, especially when the removal is punitive:

  • "The board moved to unfrock the disgraced CEO of his title and responsibilities."

However, this figurative usage is rare in everyday language. Most writers and speakers reserve "unfrock" for its original, religious context. When speaking about non-religious professional removal, words like "dismiss," "strip of rank," "oust," or "remove from office" are far more commonly used. If you ever use "unfrock" outside a religious context, it will typically be understood, but it will read as a deliberate, literary borrowing of the word for stylistic effect.

To unfrock someone is to formally and officially remove them from their position as a member of the clergy — taking away their authority, their rights, their title, and their clerical standing — as a punishment for serious misconduct. It is forced (not voluntary), institutional (requires official Church action), and permanent in nature. While occasionally used figuratively for non-religious contexts, the word is most precisely and naturally at home in religious settings.
